item.title: Condensed Matter Seminar - Emergent Quantum Phenomena in Layered Ruthenates: Insights from ARPES, Thin-Film Epitaxy, and Quantum Transport — Thu Oct 15, 11:30 AM — None
item.description: Strongly correlated oxide materials exhibit a wide range of emergent quantum phenomena arising from the interplay of charge, spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom. In this talk, I will present our recent studies of layered ruthenates using synchrotron-based angle- and spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES/SARPES), thin-film epitaxy, and quantum transport measurements. I will discuss the layer-dependent electronic structure and spin polarization of the triple-layered ruthenate Sr₄Ru₃O₁₀ [1], followed by recent advances in the epitaxial growth, strain-engineered electronic structure, and magnetotransport properties of Sr₃Ru₂O₇ thin films [2,3]. I will also highlight our development of an in situ CO₂-laser substrate preparation methodology for achieving atomically controlled oxide surfaces for high-quality epitaxial growth [4]. item.title: Are hurricanes bad for your health? Incidence of new diagnoses of physical and mental health problems in the four years after Hurricane Katrina — Thu Oct 15, 12:00 PM — SSRI-Gross Hall 270
item.description: Studies of health impacts of Hurricane Katrina have been limited in their populations covered, length of observation, and whether they included individuals no longer living in the hurricane-affected locations. In the present study, we use an event study method to investigate physical and mental health outcomes for all Black and non-Black adults who resided in the City of New Orleans just before Katrina struck, estimating outcomes in the four years after Hurricane Katrina relative to in the 10 prior years. We supplement this with estimates of physical health outcomes in the three-state region of Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi. We find pronounced spikes in first diagnoses of hypertension and emotional problems immediately after Hurricane Katrina in the four years following the hurricane. item.title: Privacy-First AI — Thu Oct 15, 1:00 PM — The TEC - Technology Engagement Center
item.description:
AI assistants are most useful when they know something about your work, and that's exactly what makes them risky. Whether you're typing a prompt, uploading a document, connecting a data source, or letting an AI agent work across your files, every interaction is a disclosure decision: student records, unpublished research, personnel matters, and confidential institutional data don't stop being sensitive just because they've entered an AI tool. This workshop builds the habit of thinking before you share, treating everything an AI system can see as a deliberate choice rather than an afterthought.
No technical background required. You'll learn to weigh what information an AI tool actually needs against the risk of sharing it - using Duke's data classification policy as a guide, alongside your own judgment about context, sensitivity, and consequences. item.title: Worlds of 1776: Genealogy and the Power of Connection in Early America — Thu Oct 15, 1:30 PM — Smith Warehouse
item.description:
Duke Professor of History Phil Stern in discussion with Karin Wulf, the Beatrice and Julio Mario Santo Domingo Director and Librarian of the John Carter Brown Library (JCB), and Professor of History at Brown University.
A historian of gender, family and politics in eighteenth-century British America, Karin Wulf earned her Ph.D. at Johns Hopkins University. Her latest book, Lineage: Genealogy and the Power of Connection in Early America (Oxford University Press, 2025) offers "a deep understanding of genealogy as a foundational element of American history, illuminating its vital role from the colonial era through the birth of the nation."
Before coming to the JCB and Brown in 2021, Wulf was the Executive Director of the Omohundro Institute of Early American History & Culture from 2013-21 and Professor of History at William & Mary.

item.title: "Eco-Derived Pigment & Material Image-Making” — Thu Oct 15, 5:00 PM — Smith Warehouse - Bay 10
item.description:
What happens when a plant becomes part of a moving image? Not only as a subject, but as a material from which an image can be made? This artist talk examines eco-derived materials as a form of tactile image-making, considering how organic and found matter can become active elements within an artist's creative process. Drawing from experiments with Peruvian maíz morado (purple corn), Bradford pear blooms, and other eco-derived materials, I will discuss approaches to material-based image-making that engage natural matter through processes of staining, layering and imprinting onto clear motion picture film leader and other surfaces. These experiments ask us to consider the role of materiality for artmaking as a site of exchange, where organic and found matter can evoke place, memory and folklore, opening alternative forms of visual storytelling.

This talk is cosponsored by the Department of Classical Studies and the Center for Jewish Studies. The talk will show how the Hebrew Bible features four laws about kinship ties between animals. In this talk, Dr. Berkowitz will read these four "animal family" laws alongside their rabbinic interpretation in order to reveal the combination of concern, cruelty, and curiosity that the ancients brought to animal lives.
Beth A. Berkowitz is Ingeborg Rennert Professor of Judaic Studies and Professor in the Department of Religion at Barnard College. item.title: State Fragmentation and the Crisis of Governance in Post-Bashir Sudan — Thu Oct 15, 6:00 PM — None
item.description:
Sudan is the site of the world's largest humanitarian crisis, yet the war that produced it is widely treated as the sudden eruption of a personal feud between two generals. This talk argues, instead, that the fighting that began in April 2023 is the culmination of a longer political history. The talk will trace the war's seeds within the Islamist regime of Omer al-Bashir (1989-2019), the 2018-19 revolution that over-threw him, the 2021 counter-revolutionary coup, and eventually the rupture between the coup plotters. The talk closes by examining Sudan's present reality-a fragmenting state with rival administrations, a war economy sustained by gold and foreign patrons, and civilian and mutual-aid networks still carrying the revolution's unfinished claims-while considering possible pathways beyond the conflict and what a sustainable peace might require.
Additional Location Information
Mai Hassan is an Associate Professor of Political Science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

"Do You Love Me" (Lana Daher, 2025, 75 min, France/Lebanon/Germany/Qatar; in French, Arabic, and English with English subtitles, DCP)
DO YOU LOVE ME is a playful and personal journey through Lebanon's audiovisual memory, composed entirely of archival footage. It is a love letter to Beirut, spanning 70 years of film, TV, home videos, and photography, exploring the Lebanese collective psyche - marked by joy and intimacy, destruction and loss. Through the eyes of citizens, filmmakers and artists (among the notable works included are films by Jocelyne Saab and Nadine Labaki), the film reconstructs a fragmented history in a country without a national archive, celebrating creative expression as both resistance, renewal and a way to preserve memory. To accompany the film, director Lana Daher has created a website, https://doyouloveme.film, which serves as an annotated index of her sources.

item.title: Duke Arts Presents: VOCES8 — Thu Oct 15, 7:30 PM — Duke Chapel
item.description:
In Lead Me Home: A Celebration of the American Choral Landscape, the celebrated British vocal ensemble VOCES8 explores the many traditions that shape American choral music. The program moves from early voices such as William Byrd to contemporary composers like Pulitzer Prize-winning North Carolina composer Caroline Shaw, with beloved spirituals like Steal Away and My Lord What a Morning woven throughout.
BBC Music Magazine praises the group's "gorgeous sound, impeccable ensemble and intense responsiveness to text, harmony and melodic shape." VOCES8 is the world's top-streaming classical vocal group and performs more than 120 concerts a year in venues from Wigmore Hall and the Concertgebouw to the Sydney Opera House. Duke Arts is proud to welcome them back to Durham with this special program as part of the We the People Initiative.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Big Woods Hike — Sun Nov 1, 9:00 AM — Big Woods Private Preserve
item.description:
Join TLC to explore a special Chatham County preserve! This will be the first public hike at Big Woods Nature Preserve, the second-largest single purchase by TLC in Chatham county. This preserve, which is not open to the public, is also TLC's first acquisition of land directly bordering Jordan Lake's protected land in a decade.
Nick Adams, TLC's Senior Land Manager West, and TLC Trail Guide, Steve Gartrell, will talk about the ecology of Big Woods and TLC's journey to acquiring the property. Due to the lack of developed trails, this hike requires traversing on uneven ground, steep inclines, and over a small stream crossing. Big Woods has a fairly open understory and rugged topography that hosts mature oak-hickory forests, mixed mesic forests, and a rich floodplain along Bush Creek. This hike will be approximately 2 miles, with about 260 feet of elevation gain. This is a free event, but preregistration is required. item.title: Porcelains and Power: The Politics of Chinese Art in the Age of American Ascendancy — Wed Nov 4, 5:30 PM — Ackland Art Museum
item.description: A talk by Dr. Ian Shin (Department of American Culture, University of Michigan), co-sponsored with the Department of History. How can we understand the relationship between art collecting and Western imperialism as more than simply a story of victim and aggressor, of the plundered and the plunderer? From the Gilded Age to World War II, elite collectors and museums in the United States transformed from owning a smattering of Chinese porcelains to possessing some of the world’s largest and most sophisticated collections of Chinese art. In this talk, historian Ian Shin shows that, beyond aesthetic taste and economics, geopolitics were vital to this transformation. This year’s theme, “We Were Never Meant to Survive: Rest, Resilience and Radical Joy,” explores how Black writers and communities use storytelling to preserve memory, imagine possibility, reclaim rest, and create joy. item.title: Trail Talks with TLC: Williamson — Fri Nov 20, 9:30 AM — Williamson Farm and Nature Preserve
item.description:
Join TLC staff for guided nature journaling at Williamson Nature Preserve! Slow down and connect with nature with Senior Volunteer and Outreach Associate, Amaya Horner! Amaya will give a brief history of Williamson Nature Preserve and talk about the types of programs that this working farm and public preserve offers. Then, we will navigate Two Ponds Loop, making stops along the way to collect observations about the world around us using nature journaling methods curated by naturalist and educator, John Muir Laws.
Please bring your own journal and writing utensils, but we will have some extra materials on hand. Participants will receive a Quick Start Guide to Nature Journaling zine written by John Muir Laws and the Wild Wonder Foundation to take home! This will be a slow, 1.5 mile hike on uneven terrain. Bring a full water bottle and a mat or blanket to sit on for the still moments on trail. This event is free, but preregistration is required.

item.title: 2nd Friday ArtWalk: Extended Museum Hours — Fri Dec 11, 5:00 PM — Ackland Art Museum
item.description:
Join us for extended hours at the Ackland Art Museum during the Carrboro-Chapel Hill 2nd Friday ArtWalk! Each month, we stay open from 5:00 – 9:00 p.m. to give visitors more time to explore. Stroll through our galleries featuring highlights from a collection of over 21,000 works of art and sketch in the galleries using art supplies from our lobby’s art cart. Admission to the Ackland is always free; no prior registration needed. Whether you’re stopping by solo or bringing friends, come be inspired during our extended open hours!
Source: UNC Chapel Hill

item.title: Home for the Holidays: A Victorian Holiday Open House of the Old Kentucky Home — Sat Dec 12, 5:00 PM — Thomas Wolfe Memorial
item.description:
Step into History This Holiday Season
Join us for the “Home for the Holidays: A Victorian Holiday Open House of the Old Kentucky Home.” Experience the warmth and charm of Holiday traditions in Thomas Wolfe’s world. Come see the home all dressed up in its Christmas finest! Guests will walk through the boardinghouse at their leisure to view this pop-up Holiday Traditions exhibit.
Enjoy holiday crafts, our exhibit hall, Christmas cookies, and warm apple cider in the Memorial’s Visitor Center. Last admission to the house is at 6:45 pm.
Source: NC Cultural Resources
